newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Lyonnaise/Suez near merger terms deal - paper.
newsitem.headline: French Lyonnaise/Suez near merger terms deal - paper.

text.p: French utilities group Lyonnaise des Eaux and conglomerate Cie de Suez are close to wrapping up the terms of a merger, notably the share parity at which they would join forces and "sweeteners" for shareholders, Le Monde newspaper said on Friday.

Both groups declined to comment on the report which quoted sources close to the case as saying the talks had already got to the stage where they "no longer concerned more than the second decimal point" of the share parity to be proposed.

Le Monde said the basis last being worked on set a parity of 41 Suez shares for 20 Lyonnaise shares and took account of a payment by Suez of nearly 3.8 billion francs ($674.6 million) in the form of a normal dividend payout and a special "premium" payment to its shareholders.

"According to our information, the financial company (Suez), which will cancel the shares it owns in itself, is preparing to pay a normal dividend of 8.20 francs per share, in other words totalling 1.27 billion francs," it said. "A 'premium' of 2.5 billion francs would be added to this," it said.

Lyonnaise, with a sprawling empire in water and electricity distribution and construction, and Suez, a conglomerate looking for a raison d'etre after selling off key assets such as Banque Indosuez, have already confirmed they are talking and that their boards will meet on April 11 to dicusss merger plans.
A Suez spokeswoman asked by Reuters about Le Monde's report reiterated that the boards were to meet next week and said: "It is out of the question to make any comment before this date".

Le Monde also said the question of the board structure for the merged group appeared to be nearing a solution where there would be a single board headed by current Lyonnaise chairman Jerome Monod until mid-1998.

In this scenario, Monod's mandate would be non-renewable and Suez chairman Gerard Mestrallet would be appointed vice-chairman and managing director of the merged group before taking over the reins from Monod in mid-1998, the newspaper said.

The newspaper report came just a day after Lyonnaise's Monod said terms for a merger had not been set and his warning that any cash payout to sweeten Suez shareholders would be clawed back when share swap parities were fixed.

Those comments suggested a tough behind-the-scenes battle between Suez shareholders, who want to recoup some of the money they have lost on the conglomerate, and Lyonnaise, which is seen to want a merger precisely because it needs Suez cash to expand.
The question of how much Suez pays out to big corporate shareholders is seen as crucial.

Jean-Louis Beffa, chairman of one of those big shareholders, the glassmaker Saint-Gobain, suggested on Tuesday that Suez pay out 3.4 billion francs. And Jean-Marie Messier, head of another shareholder, Generale des Eaux said "the figure mentioned by Mr Beffa seems to me a reasonable amount".

But it was not clear how much solidarity there was between shareholders on the precise amount of any payment. One industry source said a figure had not been discussed between all Suez shareholders and another said talks were still continuing.

Axa insurance group chairman Claude Bebear, cited by both Beffa and Messier as a supporter of their call, appears to be keeping distant. "He (Bebear) does not want to influence the decision of the Suez board, which must take this decision completely calmly," an Axa spokeswoman said on Thursday.

Le Monde also said Lyonnaise and Suez had heeded concerns voiced by Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene over the implications of a merger for Belgian ultility holding Tractebel as a result of the merger.

Tractebel is 65-percent controlled by Societe Generale de Belgique, but the latter is in turn controlled by Suez. The newspaper said the Belgian authorities had been assured that Tractebel would not suffer and remain a company quoted on the Belgian stock exchange. ($ = 5.633 French Francs)
